title: Write an Affirmation You Can Actually Act On
subtitle: Replace grand claims with a grounded statement and one next action.
description: Turn a vague positive statement into words you can presently stand behind, connect it to one action under your control, and revise the statement when it becomes false, empty, or unhelpful.
keywords: Say It Like You Mean It

lifeOsSource.hack: If an affirmation sounds false or grandiose, rewrite it as a grounded statement about a value, intention, capability, or next action you can honestly endorse today.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write the positive statement you are tempted to use, underline the part that feels exaggerated or outside your control, replace it with language you can currently stand behind, attach one concrete action that would be consistent with the statement, and review the wording after you act.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Can I honestly endorse this statement now, what action does it point to, and should I keep, narrow, or replace the wording after seeing what I actually did?

faq.question: What if an affirmation feels fake?
faq.answer: Do not force it. Narrow the wording until it describes something you can honestly endorse, such as an intention, a value, a capability you are developing, or one action you control.

faq.question: Do I have to repeat the statement a fixed number of times?
faq.answer: No. This protocol does not depend on a repetition count. The useful output is a credible statement connected to an action, followed by a check of whether the wording still fits reality.

intro.html: Positive language becomes less useful when it asks you to pretend. A stronger version is grounded: it says something you can presently endorse and points toward behavior you control. The statement is a prompt for action, not a claim that words alone change circumstances.

sections.title: 1. Write the statement you want to believe
sections.html: Start with the natural version, even when it is broad: I am confident, I finish what I start, or I can handle this. Then ask which words describe reality and which words are doing wishful work.

sections.title: 2. Ground it in something you control
sections.html: Replace absolute identity language with a value, intention, current capability, or next behavior. For example, I am always confident can become I can prepare one clear point and say it when the opportunity appears.

sections.title: 3. Attach one next action
sections.html: Choose a small action that would make the statement more concrete: draft the point, send the message, open the document, ask the question, or schedule the task. The action should remain useful even if the statement does not change how you feel.

sections.title: 4. Revise from reality
sections.html: After acting, read the statement again. Keep it if it remains honest and useful. Narrow it when it overreaches; replace it when another statement would better describe the next decision. There is no need to defend wording that no longer fits.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace therapy-adjacent framing, unsupported behavioral outcomes, fabricated first-party observations, rigid repetition schedules, and selectively presented literature claims with a bounded statement-to-action exercise.
